prize_parts.citation: For developing formal and empirically testable analysis of how electoral rules, constitutional design and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic performance.

statement.case_for: I keep B027 with Persson, Tabellini and Besley as a single part. Under the common criteria I use (conceptual originality, identification quality, maturity and attribution tractability), the programme combines a field-creating framework with about three decades of testing and a credit structure that can be described. Persson and Tabellini's synthesis of electoral rules, constitutions and fiscal outcomes forms one body of work. The Besley-Persson work on state capacity and the Besley work on political agency and selection form a second strand that the first does not subsume. A pair would credit the first strand and leave the second out of the citation, which is why I moved to the trio in round 1 and still hold it. Teorell and Enflo argued for the same trio, and I treat that as separate arguments to weigh, not as a count. What changed since round 1: the laureates and the part are unchanged, but I narrowed the citation to what is best established, namely formal analysis plus empirical tests, without claiming that every cross-country coefficient is causal. I also replaced B033 as a fallback with B024. Friberg's point that the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum strand is missing makes B033 less clean to credit than I thought in my opening. Under my own weighting, B027 and B002 are the two closest candidates. B027 is ahead on originality and maturity, and B002 is ahead on directly checkable identification. I did not rank B004 or B015 in my opening top eight, and the exchange has not changed that.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still identification. Much of the evidence on electoral rules and constitutions rests on cross-country comparisons in which adoption is endogenous, and some headline findings are sensitive to specification. As an empirical labour economist I weigh this more heavily than a theorist would, and it is why I do not call B027 a clean winner. The contribution is stronger as a framework that generated sharp, testable predictions than as a set of settled causal estimates. A second concern is thematic proximity to the 2024 institutions prize, which I treat as a timing consideration and not a scientific one. A third is that the wider political-economy field has many prominent contributors beyond the three names, so any trio is contestable. Finally, Teorell calls Besley's claim complementary rather than central, and I cannot rule out that the Committee prefers the Persson-Tabellini pair on attribution grounds.

responses.point: Teorell prefers B027 with Besley as the third name, because state capacity is a distinct strand. He also calls Besley's claim 'more complementary than central' and would accept the Persson-Tabellini pair as a fallback. He concedes that the cross-country identification is weaker than the theory, and he argues that the 2024 prize concerned the origins of institutions while B027 takes institutions as given.
responses.response: I agree on all three points, and the exchange changed how I frame the pair against the trio. I would not call Besley peripheral. His work on accountability and political selection, and the state-capacity papers with Persson, are what let the citation speak to fiscal capacity as well as to rules. I accept that the pair is the minimal fallback and I would not block it, but then the citation must be written about electoral rules and constitutions only. On the 2024 contrast, the origins-versus-operation distinction is real, but you spoke on that prize, so the Committee should test it instead of taking your word. My view is that it bears on timing, not on the science. I also lean on your point that the framework generated later designs. Quasi-experimental studies of local electoral rules and accountability are, as far as my general knowledge goes, what carries the empirical case, and I have not verified specific citations here.

responses.point: Enflo prefers the trio and says the Besley-Persson state-capacity line is not subsumed by the constitutions-and-electoral-rules programme. She says a pair would be defensible but would not cover the full discovery. She also notes that B027 and B004 face symmetric proximity worries (2024 and 2022 respectively), and she accepts that cross-country identification is less clean than in B002 or B024.
responses.response: We now agree on the trio, and your reply is part of why I settled on it. I want to qualify your symmetry point. The proximity worries are not equal in kind. For B004 the Bernanke recognition overlaps with the specific accelerator mechanism, whereas for B027 the 2024 prize concerns a different object, the origins of institutions. So I do not treat the two as mirror images. On identification I would go further than you do. The Committee should not wave it away just because the framework is influential. The citation should say 'formal and empirically testable', which is accurate, and not 'established', which overstates the cross-country results. Your point that the maturity question for B027 is largely settled is the strongest feature of the case, and it is the main reason I weigh B027 above B002 when originality and maturity are weighted together.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B002 first and B027 sixth. She argues that B002's claims come from within-family and mover designs that can be evaluated directly, whereas B027's electoral-rule results rest on weaker cross-country identification. She also points to a boundary problem with the 2024 prize and to credit divided between theory and cross-country evidence.
responses.response: I concede the identification comparison, since I made the same one in round 1. On directly checkable evidence B002 is ahead. I disagree on how much that should decide the ranking. Design credibility is one criterion, and a prize for a framework that created a field can reasonably weigh originality and decades of testing at least as heavily. I would also be careful about what 'directly evaluable' covers in B002. Mover and childhood-exposure designs rest on the assumption that the timing of moves is unrelated to child-specific shocks, and that is the part still being tested. On the chair's maturity question, the evidence that would persuade me is replication of the exposure effects in non-US register data and long-run follow-up of the cohorts. I know of extensions to other registers, but I have not verified how consistent they are. A citation limited to measurement and exposure-based designs would meet most of my maturity concern. It would not change my view that B027 is ahead on conceptual originality. B002 remains my first fallback for that reason.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B002 first with the Chetty, Hendren and Friedman trio. He keeps Katz off the three-name cap because Moving to Opportunity is an input to the causal place-effects work. He asks colleagues who press the Katz case which of the three names it would displace.
responses.response: I accept your answer on Katz as the more defensible one. I do not press the Katz case. Moving to Opportunity is an input to the neighbourhood-effects question, and Katz's stronger claim lies in the skill-premium work under B024, so crediting him in B002 would shift the discovery toward the experimental strand. My reservation about B002 is not attribution. The trio is the tightest unit on the shortlist, and I corrected my opening by giving Friedman's tax-record data construction its due weight. My reservation concerns maturity and the exposure-effect assumptions discussed above. In answer to the chair's last question, I considered a two-part configuration and rejected it. Combining B027 with B002 would need more than three unique people, so a two-part award would be unworkable under the cap.

responses.point: Friberg ranked B033 second in a way that matches my opening, and he proposed Helpman and Melitz. He argues that his reservation about B033 is attribution, not overlap with Krugman 2008, because Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related contributions and are not credited on the entry. He keeps B033 as an alternative and not as his first choice.
responses.response: The Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum point changes my fallback. In my opening I treated Krugman 2008 as the main obstacle to B033. Your argument suggests the cleaner objection is that the credited list omits a closely related strand, so a Helpman-Melitz pair would be contestable. I take that seriously and I have dropped B033 as an alternative for that reason. I agree that Melitz (2003) is distinct in content from the scale-and-variety logic of new trade theory. That makes the 2008 prize a weak objection, so I would not use it to dismiss the work. The same discipline applies to B027, where I should say the same about the 2024 prize: it is a timing consideration and not an argument about the science.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee prefers the Persson-Tabellini pair or the trio with Besley. This turns on whether the state-capacity and political-selection strand is separable from the constitutions-and-electoral-rules strand.
How much the 2024 institutions prize should count. I treat it as a timing consideration, but colleagues such as Hjalmarsson treat it as a boundary problem for attribution.

Whether later design-based work on local electoral rules and accountability is strong enough to carry the empirical case, given that the cross-country evidence is the weaker part. This rests on my general knowledge, not on verification of specific citations.

Whether B002 will pass the maturity test I described, namely replication of the exposure effects in non-US register data and long-run cohort follow-up. If it does, my ordering of B002 against B027 could change.
How to treat contributors to political economics outside the three credited names, and whether the Committee will accept any three-name cut of that field.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the credited names in B027. The profile lists no co-authorship with Persson, Tabellini or Besley. My profile records only an institutional overlap at Stockholm University (2010-17) with the IIES macro group (Hassler, Krusell), who are fellow Committee members and not candidates. Persson's association with Stockholm's IIES is general knowledge and not established by my profile, so I disclose it without treating it as a connection. A colleague's note records Persson's past committee service, and my profile does not establish anything further on that. My co-authors (Holmlund, Edin, Åslund, Öckert, Johansson, Nybom, Oosterbeek, van Ours) are not credited on any shortlisted entry. Oosterbeek and I co-authored the class-size paper that the 2021 Scientific Background cites, which is outside the shortlist. My field is empirical labour economics, so I may favour design-based evidence when judging B002 and B024, and I may weigh identification more heavily than a theorist would in judging B027. This is a disclosure only and not a recusal.
